note: Track sevenths-up, mix step 5: maj7, 7 and m7 on one root, one note moved at a time on the staff, then as three chord boxes, then named by ear in the chord game narrowed to the three 7th chords ("qualities": maj7, 7, m7), its answers named as the buttons show them. The root is moves (any key), named as {{=key}}, with a {{?key}} line, and each section has a feel to reach.

exercise.title: maj7, 7 or m7 on one root
exercise.why: From maj7 to 7 only the 7th drops a half step, and from 7 to m7 only the 3rd does, so two notes tell the three chords apart.

cells.text:
Tap {{1}}, {{3}}, {{5}} and {{7}} on the staff below: {{=key}}maj7, one note at a time. Tap it again with the ringed {{b7}} in place of {{7}}: that is {{=key}}7.
Then keep {{b7}} and tap the ringed {{b3}} in place of {{3}}: that is {{=key}}m7.
Practice until you can hum the note that moved before you tap it.

Press a chord box below to hear the chord. Go from {{=key}}maj7 to {{=key}}7 and listen for the 7th dropping, then from {{=key}}7 to {{=key}}m7 and listen for the 3rd.
Practice until you can name each of the three with your eyes closed.
{{?key}}On another root the chords have other names, and the same two notes move.

Press Start in the game below: it plays a 7th chord from any root, and you pick Major 7, Dominant 7 or Minor 7. Dominant 7 is the chord written 7, as in {{=key}}7.
Ask the same two things each time: is the 3rd major or minor, and is the 7th a half step or a whole step under the octave.
If you can't tell, press Replay in the game and hum the top note.
